title: Should You Upgrade to TypeScript 7 Yet?
summary: Should you upgrade to TypeScript 7? Compare its compiler speed, breaking changes and tool compatibility, then choose a safe migration path for your project.
body_markdown:
Upgrade to TypeScript 7 now if your project is plain TypeScript and already builds cleanly on 6.0. If you depend on typescript-eslint, Vue, Svelte, Astro, MDX or Angular template checking, run 7.0’s` tsc` alongside 6.0 and wait for 7.1 before switching fully.


The speed numbers are tempting. Then you remember that your lint pipeline, your` .vue` files and a custom codegen script all import` typescript` , and a major version bump starts to look risky.


TypeScript 7.0 shipped on July 8, 2026. This article covers what the speedup looks like, which config changes will break your build, which tools can’t use 7.0 yet, and how to run both compilers in one repo. It ends with a verdict for each type of project.


## Key Takeaways


- TypeScript 7.0 is a port of the compiler to Go, and Microsoft reports full builds 7.7x to 11.9x faster than 6.0 across five large open-source codebases.
- Every option deprecated in TypeScript 6.0, including` target: es5` ,` downlevelIteration` ,` baseUrl` ,` node10` and` classic` module resolution, and the` amd` ,` umd` and` systemjs` module formats, is a hard error in TypeScript 7.0.
- TypeScript 7.0 ships no programmatic API, so tools that import the compiler as a library, such as typescript-eslint, must keep running on 6.0 through the` @typescript/typescript6` package.
- Vue, MDX, Astro and Svelte projects should stay on TypeScript 6.0 for now, and Angular teams can use 7.0’s` tsc` in CI while keeping 6.0 in the editor.


## How Much Faster Is TypeScript 7?


TypeScript 7.0 is a port of the TypeScript compiler to Go, and Microsoft says it typically makes full builds 8x to 12x faster than TypeScript 6.0. The team did not redesign the compiler. The Go version mirrors how the original code is organised and how it works, so the two compilers give the same results. The gain comes from running as native code and from type-checking on several threads that share memory.


These are the full-build figures from[Microsoft’s TypeScript 7.0 announcement](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/) :


Codebase TypeScript 6 TypeScript 7 Speedup


vscode 125.7s 10.6s 11.9x


sentry 139.8s 15.7s 8.9x


bluesky 24.3s 2.8s 8.7x


playwright 12.8s 1.47s 8.7x


tldraw 11.2s 1.46s 7.7x


Microsoft ran these builds with the default of four type-checker workers (` --checkers 4` ) on large open-source codebases. The announcement does not say what hardware it used. The lowest result, tldraw at 7.7x, falls just under the “8x to 12x” range Microsoft states.


The time TypeScript 7 actually saves depends on how big your codebase is. Working from Microsoft’s figures, vscode saves about 115 seconds per full build and tldraw saves under 10. A small app that already type-checks in two seconds will speed up by a similar ratio but save very little time.


Three smaller changes, one line each:


- ` --checkers` and` --builders` control parallel type-checking and project-reference builds. The 7.0 release notes call both flags experimental.
- ` --watch` now runs on a Go port of Parcel’s file watcher.
- JS and JSDoc checking was reworked to behave more like` .ts` analysis. The details are in[the typescript-go CHANGES.md](https://github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/blob/main/CHANGES.md) .


## What Breaks When You Upgrade From TypeScript 5.x or 6.0


Code that has no errors on TypeScript 6.0, with` stableTypeOrdering` turned on and` ignoreDeprecations` removed, should give the same output on TypeScript 7.0. Everything that breaks comes from 6.0: 7.0 inherits 6.0’s new defaults, and anything 6.0 marked as deprecated now stops the build. Teams coming straight from 5.x take on both sets of changes at once.


### New Defaults


Four TypeScript 7.0 defaults, carried over from 6.0, cause most of the breakage:


- ` strict` is` true` . Expect new errors in loosely typed code. Well-typed helpers built from[TypeScript utility types](https://blog.openreplay.com/typescript-utility-types/) make the transition easier.
- ` module` defaults to` esnext` .
- ` rootDir` defaults to` ./` . If your` tsconfig.json` sits above` src` , set` rootDir` explicitly.
- ` types` defaults to` \[\]` . List global type packages such as` node` or` jest` by name, or set` \["*"\]` to get the old behaviour back.


Four more defaults changed:` target` now tracks the newest finished ECMAScript edition (one step behind` esnext` ),` noUncheckedSideEffectImports` is` true` ,` libReplacement` is` false` , and` stableTypeOrdering` is` true` and can’t be turned off.


### Deprecations That Are Now Hard Errors


The TypeScript 7.0 release notes list twelve deprecated options and behaviours that are now hard errors:


- ` target: es5`
- ` downlevelIteration`
- ` moduleResolution: node` /` node10` (use` nodenext` or` bundler` )
- ` moduleResolution: classic` (use` bundler` or` nodenext` )
- ` module: amd` ,` umd` ,` systemjs` ,` none` (use` esnext` or` preserve` )
- ` baseUrl` (write` paths` relative to the project root)
- ` esModuleInterop` or` allowSyntheticDefaultImports` set to` false`
- ` alwaysStrict` set to` false`
- The` module` keyword in namespace declarations
- ` asserts` on imports (use` with` )
- ` /// <reference no-default-lib />` under` skipDefaultLibCheck`
- File paths passed on the command line when the directory has a` tsconfig.json` , unless you add` --ignoreConfig`


` outFile` is not on that list, but it is gone too. The 6.0 release notes say 6.0 already removed it, and that every option 6.0 deprecated is removed entirely in 7.0. If you still use` outFile` , move that job to a bundler.


There is also a type-level change: inferring from template literal types no longer splits a character such as an emoji into two halves. You’ll only notice this if you wrote type-level string helpers that relied on the old UTF-16 splitting.


Here is a typical legacy config and the version that works on 7.0:


```text
// Before: hard errors on 7.0
{
"  compilerOptions  "  : {
"  target  "  :   "  es5  "  ,                 // error: es5 unsupported
"  downlevelIteration  "  :   true  ,      // error: removed
"  moduleResolution  "  :   "  node  "  ,      // error: node/node10 unsupported
"  baseUrl  "  :   "  ./src  "  ,              // error: baseUrl unsupported
"  paths  "  : {   "  @/*  "  : [  "  *  "  ] }
},
"  include  "  : [  "  ./src  "  ]
}
```


```text
// After: valid on 7.0
{
"  compilerOptions  "  : {
"  moduleResolution  "  :   "  bundler  "  ,
"  rootDir  "  :   "  ./src  "  ,
"  types  "  : [  "  node  "  ,   "  jest  "  ],
"  paths  "  : {   "  @/*  "  : [  "  ./src/*  "  ] }
},
"  include  "  : [  "  ./src  "  ]
}
```


The new version drops` target` so the default applies, points` paths` at the project root, and sets` rootDir` and` types` explicitly.


Microsoft recommends moving to 6.0 first. Upgrade to 6.0, fix every deprecation warning (the[TypeScript 6.0 announcement](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-6-0/) explains each one), remove` ignoreDeprecations` , and only then install 7.0.


## Which Tools Don’t Work With TypeScript 7 Yet?


Tools that import the TypeScript compiler as a library, and the tools behind Vue, MDX, Astro, Svelte and Angular template checking, don’t work with TypeScript 7.0 yet, because TypeScript 7.0 does not ship a programmatic API. According to Microsoft’s 7.0 announcement, tools that import the compiler as a library, such as typescript-eslint, must keep running on TypeScript 6.0 through the` @typescript/typescript6` compatibility package. If your[type-aware linting with typescript-eslint](https://blog.openreplay.com/lint-typescript-eslint/) setup relies on a peer dependency on` typescript` , it needs the alias setup described in the next section.


Embedded languages are also affected. Microsoft’s 7.0 announcement says Vue, MDX, Astro and Svelte projects should stay on TypeScript 6.0 for now. Volar and similar tools build TypeScript support into those file formats by calling the compiler directly, and 7.0 has no API for them to call. Angular template type-checking has the same limitation. For Angular, the announcement suggests a split: use 7.0’s` tsc` from the command line and in CI to catch errors across the whole project quickly, and leave 6.0 in charge of the editor so template checking keeps working.


In VS Code, Microsoft’s dedicated TypeScript 7 extension has two command palette commands, “Disable TypeScript 7 Language Server” and “Enable TypeScript 7 Language Server”, so you can move the editor between 6.0 and 7.0 whenever you need to. If the editor starts misbehaving after the switch, the usual[TypeScript debugging workflow in VS Code](https://blog.openreplay.com/debugging-typescript-with-visual-studio-code/) still applies.


Microsoft plans to add an API back in TypeScript 7.1, though it won’t match the old one. That release is the realistic point for these integrations to move over.


## How to Run TypeScript 7 and 6.0 Side by Side


To run both versions in one repo, use npm aliases. Point the` typescript` package name at the 6.0 compatibility package, and install 7.0 under a different name. Tools that import` typescript` then load 6.0. The compatibility package gives you the 6.0 API plus a 6.0 command called` tsc6` .


In a plain npm project,` npx tsc` then runs 7.0. There is a catch. The compatibility package depends on a full copy of TypeScript 6.0 that declares its own` tsc` , so two packages compete for that command name. Users have[reported that Yarn and Bun can link tsc to 6.0](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/63634) instead. The` typecheck` script below calls the 7.0 file directly, so it doesn’t depend on which package wins the` tsc` name. This is the setup Microsoft describes, shown here with scripts:


```text
{
"  devDependencies  "  : {
"  @typescript/native  "  :   "  npm:typescript@^7.0.2  "  ,
"  typescript  "  :   "  npm:@typescript/typescript6@^6.0.2  "
},
"  scripts  "  : {
"  typecheck  "  :   "  node node_modules/@typescript/native/bin/tsc --noEmit  "  ,
"  typecheck:6  "  :   "  tsc6 --noEmit  "  ,
"  lint  "  :   "  eslint .  "
}
}
```


` typecheck` runs 7.0.` typecheck:6` runs 6.0, which is useful for checking that both compilers agree during migration.` lint` resolves` typescript` to 6.0 through the alias. To set up the 6.0 alias from the terminal instead, run` npm install -D typescript@npm:@typescript/typescript6` . If you only do that, you get` tsc6` and nothing else, so add the 7.0 alias as well.


Run` npx tsc --version` to see which compiler a plain` tsc` calls. Microsoft only documents this setup for npm, so check the result yourself if you use pnpm, Yarn or Bun.


## Should You Upgrade? The Verdict by Situation


Whether to upgrade to TypeScript 7 depends on two things: how clean your 6.0 build is, and whether anything in your toolchain imports the compiler.


Situation What to do Why


New project Adopt 7.0 You have no legacy config and get the new defaults from day one


Small plain-TS codebase Upgrade after a clean 6.0 build A clean 6.0 build carries over to 7.0 with identical results


Large monorepo, custom tooling, or Vue/Svelte/Astro/MDX/Angular 7.0` tsc` in CI, 6.0 for tools and editor Tools and embedded languages need an API that 7.0 lacks


**New project:** start on 7.0. If you’re migrating from Flow to TypeScript, aim for 7.0’s defaults from the start so you don’t have to migrate a second time.


**Small plain-TS codebase:** go to 6.0, fix every deprecation, then switch. The time saved will be small, but you’ll be on the maintained line.


**Large monorepo:** set up the alias, move CI type-checking to 7.0’s` tsc` now, and keep linting, codegen and the editor on 6.0 until 7.1 ships its API.


## Conclusion


TypeScript 7.0 type-checks your code almost exactly as 6.0 does, only faster. Nearly everything that breaks comes from 6.0’s deprecations or from tools that need a compiler API. Start by getting a clean build on 6.0 with no` ignoreDeprecations` . After that, either switch completely or add the npm alias and let CI run 7.0’s` tsc` while your tooling stays on 6.0 until 7.1.


## FAQs


Is tsgo or @typescript/native-preview the same thing as TypeScript 7?


Not any more. Before 7.0 shipped, the Go compiler was previewed in the @typescript/native-preview package, and its command was tsgo. The last version of that package is 7.0.0-dev.20260707.2, published the day before the stable release. In TypeScript 7.0 the native compiler lives in the regular typescript package and runs as tsc. Nightly builds now come from typescript@next, so change tsgo to tsc in your CI scripts.


Does TypeScript 7 make Vite, esbuild or SWC builds faster?


No. Vite, esbuild and SWC turn TypeScript into JavaScript by removing the types without checking them, so they never call tsc and their transpile times stay the same. TypeScript 7 speeds up the separate type-check step, usually tsc --noEmit in CI or a pre-commit hook, and the editor language server. If type-checking is not the slowest step in your pipeline, upgrading will not make builds noticeably shorter.


Does ts-node work with TypeScript 7?


Not directly. ts-node compiles files through the TypeScript compiler API, and 7.0 does not ship that API. With the npm alias setup, ts-node's import of typescript resolves to the 6.0 compatibility package, so it keeps running on 6.0 while tsc runs 7.0. For code that uses only erasable syntax, Node.js type stripping in recent versions can run .ts files with no compiler at all, but it does no type-checking.


Can TypeScript 7 still compile to ES5 for older browsers?


No. TypeScript 6.0 raised the lowest supported target to ES2015 and deprecated target es5. In 7.0, target es5 is a hard error. If you still need ES5 output, have tsc emit ES2015 or later and post-process the result with Babel or another compiler. Alternatively, compile the TypeScript source directly with that external tool.
